Use grouped keys for request intake, clarification, consent, dispatch, delay, arrival, offered action, declined action, supply handoff, return, discrepancy, follow-up, and closure. Text variants should preserve the same action meaning. A request for a visit cannot become implied consent because one localization uses a softer verb.

Dialogue can show distinct roles through what each person knows: the dispatcher knows routes and schedules, the quartermaster knows accepted stock, the receiver knows their own preference, and the medical owner provides authoritative care results. A character never explains another owner’s private state unless they were given that information legitimately.

### Field 09 expansion — measurements for decision quality

Record if the player could distinguish request from diagnosis, reservation from consumption, arrival from completed care, and contact permission from treatment consent. Also record whether the player knew why a visit was deferred, whether the operation could be safely abandoned, and whether the return summary reconciled goods. These observations inform UI and content revisions before balance tuning.

The technical profile uses varied operation lengths, request counts, item counts, route updates, and history sizes. Compare active and closed records separately. Any performance change must preserve which operation updates first and how same-day owner results are displayed.

### Field 10 expansion — field-language review

The final review sheet pairs each UI status with its generating owner, exact receipt, dialogue key, accessibility label, and next action. The prose reviewer checks tone and clarity; a medical systems reviewer checks that no text implies unsupported diagnosis or treatment; and an integrator checks transaction and save behavior.

The operation pack moves forward with one complete route and a small set of repeatable request templates. Remaining destinations and side quests stay in the authoring backlog until the first route survives cancellation, restore, route delay, refusal, and inventory reconciliation without duplicated state.

## Pass 9 — Complete route rehearsal and field encounter bank

### Field 01 expansion — full North Depot rehearsal

**Before departure:** the player reads two request notes, confirms which is newer, and sees that one contact asked for a visit while another asked only for a sealed delivery. The player selects a responder and driver from current eligibility results, reserves the listed case and supplies through inventory, and confirms a route with the expedition owner.

**On the route:** the team receives a delay. The player may wait for the depot window, request a supported alternate route, or return. If the player waits, arrival is confirmed by the expedition owner. At the site, the contact confirms the visit but limits which family detail can be shared. The player records that boundary, chooses one currently supported care action, and hands over the sealed parcel as a separate inventory transaction. If the contact refuses the care action, the parcel task can still complete.

**After departure:** the team returns with one unused item. Inventory accepts the return. The operation summary shows the accepted care result, the refusal or consent boundary, the transfer receipt, the actual travel duration, and the unresolved request. The next campaign-day callback appears only if the contact permitted follow-up.

### Field 02 expansion — decision outcomes in the rehearsal

| Decision point | Choice | Immediate result | Later consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Request review | Accept visit | Team can be prepared | Visit window becomes actionable |
| Request review | Ask for more information | No team or stock committed | Request remains open |
| Dispatch | Assign eligible team | Duty owner confirms | Home roster shows absence |
| Dispatch | No eligible team | Operation cannot leave | Deferral reason remains visible |
| Route delay | Wait | Expedition advances under current route | Arrival may miss the window |
| Route delay | Return | Team comes back if accepted | Visit closes with interruption |
| Contact | Ask before visit | Preference is recorded | Care task may continue or stop |
| Care | Recipient declines | No care mutation | Parcel can remain separately accepted |
| Supply | Transfer parcel | Inventory receipt created | Site confirms handoff |
| Return | Return unused item | Inventory reconciliation | Case closes with accurate quantity |

### Field 03 expansion — case and encounter row bank

| Candidate | Local context | Playable action |
|---|---|---|
| depot_contact_shift | Contact has a changing work hour | Confirm a time before dispatch |
| clinic_room_reassigned | Site changes receiving room | Inspect the alternate room |
| sealed_case_unclaimed | Parcel has no recipient receipt | Trace custody |
| remote_contact_no_reply | Radio contact is quiet | Wait or close with retry condition |
| driver_requests_return | Route window becomes unsafe | Request return |
| supply_label_conflict | Two item labels disagree | Verify catalog and owner |
| family_requests_privacy | Relative asks what will be shared | Set specific contact boundary |
| work_party_changes_location | Crew moves between known sites | Reconfirm destination |
| second_witness_available | Another source arrives | Compare without overwriting |
| receiving_site_closed | Access changes after dispatch | Return or request new access |
| old_referral_reappears | Prior request returns | Check whether it is still open |
| case_latch_damaged | Equipment condition is uncertain | Inspect and use accepted alternative |
| local_helper_offers_route | Resident offers guidance | Verify with expedition/map owner |
| report_arrives_late | Message postdates original request | Reassess before acting |
| returned_goods_unmatched | Inventory receipt differs | Reconcile or flag discrepancy |
| followup_window_passed | Contact is no longer available | Close honestly or ask later |

### Field 04 expansion — character web and scene order

The field team can include a responder and driver; the receiving contact can appear in more than one story only if they remain at that location. A local steward can help transfer sealed goods but cannot grant consent on behalf of another person. A relative can request contact but cannot rewrite a patient’s recorded preference. These role boundaries inform scene writing and prevent accidental omniscience.

Use the five storylines in flexible order. A Last Return Slip can be found at the home base after any route. The Parcel Left Outside begins only when an inventory transfer is unresolved. A Seat for the Returned begins from a specific contact request. The Fever Road needs evidence from two sources. The Quiet Queue needs more than one request that can legitimately compete for a window.

### Field 05 expansion — operation encounter bank

| Encounter | Choice | Valid result |
|---|---|---|
| contact at the wrong hour | wait, reschedule, or close | New availability or no contact |
| recipient asks who sent the team | disclose permitted source or defer | Contact understood or remains private |
| item is overpacked | remove item or reduce task list | Inventory plan updated before dispatch |
| route contact suggests a shortcut | verify or decline | Expedition result controls travel |
| local helper wants a role | query eligibility or thank them | Assignment accepted or not made |
| recipient asks to speak alone | grant privacy or stop visit | Consent boundary recorded |
| steward disputes parcel count | recount and compare receipt | Inventory difference resolved or open |
| team arrives after window | request new permission | New visit or safe return |
| contact gives a corrected date | compare source history | Request revision recorded |
| team member is unavailable | reassign or cancel | Duty owner confirms |
| family asks for a message | review sharing boundary | Message sent only if allowed |
| receiving room is occupied | inspect alternate site | Site readiness result |

### Field 06 expansion — owner response ledger

The rehearsal ledger links each decision to its owner: request state to current quest/campaign authority; team eligibility to duty; load and transfer to inventory; route and arrival to expedition; medical action to medical; privacy and contact preference to the current narrative/relationship contract; history to the existing archive or journal surface. The operation record holds correlation references, not copied values.

For the save rehearsal, capture immediately before dispatch, after accepted reservations, after the route delay, after the field action, and after return but before closeout. At each point, reload and verify the operation asks owners for current receipts rather than repeating effects.

### Field 07 expansion — screen sequence and focus

The route view has a stable sequence: requests; destination; team; supplies; route; confirmation. After confirmation, replace the preparation controls with live-operation controls. At a route result, announce the change and keep focus on the same operation. At arrival, move focus only when the player chooses the contact interaction. Closeout returns focus to the request card that generated the route.

If the operation can be minimized under existing panel routing, it remains visible as a small status card with destination, stage, and blocker. It does not keep a modal open or prevent normal campaign play.

### Field 08 expansion — encounter text shapes

Keep field encounters actionable and grounded. “The depot steward says the crate is dry and still sealed. The transfer slip has no receiver mark.” This gives the player a fact and a next step. Avoid “The town urgently needs help” if no source identifies what action is wanted. Dialogue can convey fear or fatigue but should not convert mood into an unowned medical state.

The closeout uses the same terms as the board. “Visit declined” means the person chose not to receive the offered visit. “No contact” means the team did not reach them. “Route interrupted” means no arrival occurred. These labels should not be collapsed in prose or analytics.

### Field 09 expansion — route rehearsal measures

Measure time to prepare the route, owner query count, reservation and return consistency, operation save size, time to open history, and number of manual refreshes needed after an owner result. Conduct a comprehension pass: ask the player which items are committed, whether the person consented, and which tasks remain open.

The route is balanced when preparation has meaningful alternatives and an honest no-dispatch path. Do not shorten the route solely to improve completion rate. Preserve the player’s ability to reduce scope or decline work.

### Field 10 expansion — implementation packet boundary

The first implementation candidate consists of one route with no more than two stops, one care result supported by the current medical system, one separately reconciled transfer, one route delay, one refusal, and one return callback. A second package can add the broader encounter bank.

The package is blocked if inventory cannot reconcile returns, expedition cannot resume from a saved stage, medical cannot accept the intended caller, or the UI cannot preserve privacy boundaries. Record the exact unmet contract and leave the route content disabled until the owner accepts it.

## Pass 10 — Route continuity and campaign handoff detail

### Field 01 expansion — operation resumes

When the player returns to an active operation, summarize the current stage, last owner result, next valid action, and expected home-duty impact. If no result arrived, say that the operation is still waiting. Do not imply that time passed for an away team unless the campaign clock and expedition owners advanced.

### Field 02 expansion — operation changes

Changing a dispatched operation requires checking whether the new task, route, person, and item are still valid. The player can remove a stop, request a new one, or return if the owning expedition contract permits it. The operation presents which reservations or assignments will be released before committing the change.

### Field 03 expansion — compact data rows

| Candidate | Current stage | Change request | Receipt |
|---|---|---|---|
| route_remove_stop | Traveling or planned | Cancel one unvisited request | Quest/expedition update |
| route_add_followup | Returned | Add a consented visit | New request reference |
| route_replace_member | Before departure | Reassign eligible worker | Duty owner result |
| route_return_goods | Returned | Reconcile unused items | Inventory receipt |
| route_close_no_contact | No contact after valid attempt | Close with reason | Quest closeout |
| route_rebook_window | Contact permits another visit | Select a supported date | Calendar/quest result |

### Field 04 expansion — continuity after decline

If a recipient declines, future content uses the recorded boundary. It can offer a new opportunity only when a new request or explicit permission exists. A declined visit does not become a recurring random prompt. The person can change their preference through a supported interaction, and the player can see the source of that change.

### Field 05 expansion — story follow-up cards

Add callbacks for a corrected request, a returned case, a missed route, a successfully private visit, an unanswered contact, and a new agreed time. Each callback has its source receipt, earliest time, cancel condition, and visible result. It may close with no new request.

### Field 06 expansion — restoration check

The restore review compares operation stage with inventory, duty, expedition, medical, and quest receipts. If one owner is unavailable, the operation remains unresolved and does not replay the last mutation. The player sees a recoverable state or an explicit integrity message through the current save owner.

### Field 07 expansion — safe exit behavior

Closing the operation panel never cancels travel. A separate command cancels or returns only when the current operation supports it. The panel remembers the selected stop and returns focus to it after the player inspects a receipt.

### Field 08 expansion — summary labels

Use distinct labels for requested, scheduled, dispatched, arrived, offered, accepted, declined, transferred, returned, interrupted, and closed. These terms represent different facts and cannot be collapsed into one “complete” badge.

### Field 09 expansion — route audit questions

Review whether one operation can survive a missed visit, a delayed route, a team member change, a refused action, unused goods, and a save/load break. Measure how many refreshes are needed for all owners to display the same result.

### Field 10 expansion — handoff deliverables

The package includes an operation timeline, correlation references, save-stage matrix, item flow, permission copy, callback sheet, and route UI state list. It reports current word count separately from the number of validated and reachable records.

## Pass 11 — Mobile outreach route book, encounter receipts, and referral story set

This pass extends the same ten fields with a route-centered content workbook. It remains provisional until current health, inventory, travel, roster, journal, radio, and save owners are checked. The outreach team does not become a second clinic, patient database, triage authority, or treatment simulator. The plan describes player-visible work and the handoffs needed to make it real. No clinical outcomes or item quantities below are authoritative.

### Field 01 expansion — the route is a promise of access

A mobile visit has value when the player understands where the team can go, whom it intends to meet, what the visit can and cannot provide, and what will happen if the route or requested service is unavailable. Route planning therefore has three layers: proposed stops, owner-confirmed travel and access, and confirmed follow-up. The first layer is authored intent. The second belongs to current map/travel and site-access owners. The third belongs to the system that actually accepted a service, referral, or delivery.

An outreach day begins with an itinerary and a readiness explanation. It does not begin by silently consuming inventory or advancing time. The player can inspect each stop, its source, expected contact, unresolved access note, and known constraints. If the roster or travel owner refuses a route, show the exact reason and permit a supported alternative: move the visit, send a message through an existing channel, or record the stop as deferred. Never let a panel claim that a vehicle, clinician, medicine, or service is available merely because the scenario text mentions one.

The route summary should distinguish a planned visit, a departed team, an arrival, a completed encounter, and an unresolved follow-up. Each state must come from a real owner receipt or remain visibly a draft intention. The player can understand a failed visit without mistaking a failed interaction for lost data.

### Field 02 expansion — encounter contract and data boundary

A candidate encounter card carries a visit reference, resident or group reference where current privacy rules permit, place reference, source of the request, conversation topic, consent status if a current owner supports it, action attempted, owner response, and follow-up obligation. Treat the card as an interaction record rather than a mutable clinical chart. Health state remains in its current owner. Do not create symptoms, diagnoses, treatment plans, or hidden patient scores in authored content.

Information states must be precise. “The resident asked for a visit” is different from “the resident agreed to discuss a concern.” “The team arrived” is different from “the service was delivered.” “A referral was offered” is different from “a receiving service accepted it.” The interface should never imply a completed medical intervention if the only fact is that a conversation occurred.

Candidate outcome vocabulary: welcomed, declined, deferred, inaccessible, referred, service-confirmed, follow-up-needed, and unresolved. These are draft presentation labels, not an instruction to add a new state machine. Reuse an equivalent current contract when it exists. If there is no owner for a proposed transition, record it as a narrative note and keep the task unintegrated.

### Field 03 expansion — route stop cards for distinct settings

| Working stop | Request source | Visit purpose | Completion evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glasshouse Row | A gardener asks for a private check-in after several difficult shifts | Offer a conversation and establish whether a supported service is requested | The resident’s response is recorded without assigning a diagnosis |
| West Pump Rooms | A maintenance crew asks for a scheduled visit before a long work rotation | Confirm that the team reached the work site and ask what follow-up they want | Arrival is sourced from travel; follow-up is accepted by its owner |
| Ferryless Landing | A family reports that the usual route is impassable | Check route evidence, notify the household, and reschedule if needed | A current travel result or a clear deferred status |
| Lantern School | A teacher requests a group information session | Provide a plain-language session through an available interaction and capture questions | Attendance is not treated as individual consent |
| North Relay Cabin | A radio operator asks to speak away from the console | Offer a private visit and preserve an optional return channel | The person chooses whether to leave a follow-up message |
| Orchard Shed | A seasonal worker requests a supply check | Compare the request with canonical inventory and approved distribution rules | Inventory owner confirms any actual transfer |
| Lower Tunnel Gate | A crew asks for an outreach stop before a hazardous shift | Verify access and roster safety gates before proposing a visit | The duty/travel owner accepts or refuses the itinerary |
| Old Weigh House | A resident asks for help locating a known service provider | Explain the existing referral route and ask permission to send a message | A message-delivery receipt, or an unaccepted referral marked clearly |
| Windward Stalls | Several traders ask for a short group meeting | Give the group a neutral overview and offer private follow-up | Group attendance and individual follow-up remain separate |
| Quarry Margin | An isolated worker has missed two check-ins | Attempt contact using an existing route or communication owner | No presumption about why the worker is absent |
| Ash Court | A household requests a second visit after a previous appointment was deferred | Reconfirm availability and keep the earlier deferment visible | New visit status references the earlier receipt |
| Cold Store Office | A custodian asks for an inventory reconciliation conversation | Review authorized supplies and identify a responsible current owner | No stock changes without the inventory command |
| Watchline Shelter | A night-shift group asks for a visit outside the normal window | Evaluate existing roster/time constraints and offer a supported time | A real accepted appointment or a readable refusal |
| South Water Steps | A resident wants help reporting an access barrier | Capture the barrier and route it to the current site/travel authority | A tracked report with an owner response or stated wait |
| Signal Yard | A group asks for a relay message to another settlement | Use a currently available radio/message channel | Delivered, queued, or failed receipt from the channel owner |

The table creates a pool, not a requirement that all stops appear in one campaign. Early content should select a small number of stops whose access path, interaction, and receipt are already supportable. The others remain authoring candidates with explicit dependency notes.

### Field 04 expansion — outreach stories with different sources of tension

**The missed appointment.** A resident declined a previous visit because they were repairing a shared roof and did not want a team arriving in front of neighbors. The next scene lets the player offer an appointment in a quieter location or leave a message. The resident may accept, defer, or decline. None is framed as a failure. If a visit occurs, the closeout focuses on whether the person got the contact they asked for and what follow-up they authorized. The story teaches that access and timing matter.

**The route ledger.** A local driver has recorded several disagreements between maps and actual travel conditions. A mobile team wants to keep a dependable itinerary, while residents do not want every private footpath entered into a public record. The player can review the source and audience of each route note. A choice can publish a general travel warning, preserve a private note, or defer a claim. The story does not turn residents into map data; it makes consent and information audience part of the work.

**The waiting room without a room.** A teacher coordinates an information session for families, but the proposed school building is unavailable after roof damage. The team must find an existing accessible meeting point and make clear which topics can be discussed publicly and which require a private conversation. A successful session may produce several follow-up requests, but attendance never substitutes for consent. The ending shows the teacher adapting a reusable schedule rather than receiving a miraculous facility.

**The message that cannot be delivered.** A worker asks the team to send a personal message to a distant relative. The normal relay is down. The player can hold a note for an authorized later delivery or explain the failure and ask what the sender prefers. A story branch occurs only if a current message owner records a real delivery. If no route exists, the emotional resolution is honesty and a chosen alternative, not a fake success toast.

### Field 05 expansion — service and follow-up task deck

Tasks should have one meaningful action and one explicit receipt. Candidate deck:

1. Review tomorrow’s planned stops and flag an unverified route.
2. Ask a household whether it wants a visit, a message, or no contact.
3. Move an appointment to a supported location.
4. Record that a resident declined further discussion.
5. Carry an authorized message through the current radio owner.
6. Reconcile a requested supply against current inventory.
7. Confirm whether the team reached the named site.
8. Return to a household that requested a second visit.
9. Send a route-access concern to the appropriate current owner.
10. Offer a private follow-up after a group information session.
11. Record that a receiving service did not accept the referral.
12. Ask the sender whether a delayed message should remain queued.
13. Check whether an earlier request is still wanted before repeating it.
14. Close a duplicate stop request by linking it to the original receipt.
15. Explain why an appointment window cannot be supported by current duty constraints.
16. Leave a non-sensitive notice with permission when a resident is away.
17. Revisit a stop after a route owner updates access information.
18. Capture a question that the team cannot answer and identify the next owner.
19. Return unused authorized supplies through inventory’s existing receipt.
20. Close the day with completed, deferred, refused, and unresolved visits separated.

Do not grant generic relationship, health, or morale rewards for a respectful action. If an existing relationship owner receives a supported conversation event, its outcome must use that contract. The game may still communicate that the player honored a request through narrative, journal, and a clear service-history receipt.

### Field 06 expansion — integration fit and existing-plan coordination

Before promoting a stop, check its expected seam across six areas: map/travel, roster and duty fitness, canonical inventory, health or medical service, relationship or cohort privacy, and journal/radio follow-up. Each area may have a different owner. A route plan is not an invitation to combine them into a new manager. Identify the smallest interaction path: UI intent, current host adapter, owner command, emitted result, save owner if the result is stateful, and visible player feedback.

The plan should maintain a dependency matrix with statuses: verified current API, needs premise check, blocked by missing owner, content only, or rejected as duplicate. A status requires a source path and a date during implementation. Integration plans that are complete remain complete. A candidate stop that resembles a sealed medical, radio, map, trade, or accessibility plan does not reopen it. A new package needs a new, specific evidence claim and a narrow path owner.

Data authoring must use the current schema and validator. The provisional card fields above are not a JSON schema. Do not create a parallel catalog merely because content authors want a convenient file. If the current medical or quest catalog has a suitable extension point, propose it with its owning maintainer and preserve existing validation.

### Field 07 expansion — itinerary, stop, and service history views

The route panel needs a day overview, a stop detail, a service history, and a deferred list. The day overview shows proposed stops and constraints in route order only if current route data supports order. Stop detail separates request, permission, access, and available action. Service history shows what was attempted and the result. Deferred list explains which owner update or player action can make each stop actionable again.

The panel should not duplicate the canonical route or patient state. It asks owners for an immutable presentation snapshot or current query. Selection can be transient UI state; it must not become persistent gameplay authority. When the panel closes, it restores focus. A stop whose status changes while open updates without moving focus unexpectedly. If two events arrive for the same stop, the history may show both with timestamps or simulation steps and source labels; it should not collapse them into an unexplained new summary.

Costly transfers, appointment cancellation, or irreversible sharing of a private note require a review of the current owner’s confirmation conventions. Less consequential navigation does not. A disabled action explains its actual missing precondition and offers a valid next step.

### Field 08 expansion — dignity, access, and readable failure

The outreach loop should let a resident decline without penalty, preserve the choice, and avoid repeated unwanted prompts. Private topics remain private in the interface and are not exposed on a group briefing screen. If a message or note has an audience, show that audience before commit. The copy must distinguish inability to reach someone from refusal, and a refusal from a declined service.

Candidate copy examples:

- “The household asked to choose another day.”
- “The resident did not want to discuss this today.”
- “The team arrived, but the building was unavailable.”
- “The message is queued. It has not been delivered.”
- “The referral was offered; no receiving service has confirmed it.”
- “The supply request exceeds the stock shown by inventory.”
- “The stop is deferred because the route has not been verified.”
- “The earlier request is still open. Ask before scheduling another visit.”

Review keyboard and controller focus, scalable text within current support, clear non-color status, readable notification timing, and interruption behavior. Do not call an optional privacy choice a “bonus objective.” Do not make the player repeatedly click through refusal dialogue to clear an alert. Any accessibility expansion requiring a new preference or core contract must be routed to that authority rather than added locally.

### Field 09 expansion — schedule, catalog, and long-session behavior

The route book can grow without making each daily update expensive. Load authored descriptions through the established catalog lifecycle; resolve available stops from current owner queries; render only visible cards; and refresh on route, roster, inventory, service, or message events where those events already exist. Avoid a per-frame check across all residents. A bulk update should not rewrite old encounter history.

Proposed bounded profiles for future measurement include: one stop with no follow-up; several stops with mixed responses; an unavailable route; a team member removed by the current duty owner; a supply request that changes before confirmation; and a save taken after arrival but before service confirmation. A long-session profile should examine a growing encounter history, duplicated requests, repeated declined visits, and queued messages. Track query counts, render time, history size, and the number of commands that fail due to stale previews. No performance target is claimed until measured on a named build and machine.

Replay should reproduce the same route and authored prompt ordering under the current deterministic owner contracts. Do not generate visit ordering from unordered collection iteration. If the game’s existing random-choice contract applies to a narrative variant, store or reproduce its seed inputs through the current owner. Repeated playback should not create duplicate visit receipts.

### Field 10 expansion — first playable outreach slice

The first slice is a single itinerary with three stops: one completed conversation, one resident-chosen deferment, and one inaccessible route. It includes a day overview, one detail card, one completion/deferment receipt, one journal history entry, and a save/resume checkpoint only if the affected owner already has a supported save contract. It does not need a full health simulation to demonstrate a truthful outreach loop.

Acceptance evidence should answer:

- Which current owner authorizes the team’s route?
- Who determines that the team has arrived?
- Which system owns any inventory transfer?
- Where is consent or refusal recorded, if supported?
- What exact result is visible after save and reload?
- Can one stop be disabled without breaking the other two?
- Does a declined visit stay closed unless the resident reopens it?
- Are group attendance and private follow-up separate?
- Can the player distinguish queued communication from delivery?
- Can an unavailable medical action explain its actual dependency without inventing a substitute?

The slice is ready to integrate only after a named owner accepts the package, the exact files are claimed, data validity is demonstrated, and the end-to-end receipt agrees with the current Core, host, UI, and save contracts.


## Pass 12 — Visit protocol workbook, continuity cards, and mobile service closeout

This pass supplies more execution-level structure for authored outreach days. All medical or logistical effects still require current owner contracts. The plan adds no diagnosis rules, clinical state, private chart, medicine store, or substitute appointment authority.

### Field 01 expansion — outreach run lengths and stop boundaries

A single-stop outing tests whether the team can reach and respectfully close one visit. A half-day outing adds a planned stop, an access change, and a reschedule. A multi-day outreach arc includes a return visit, an optional referral, and an end-of-day reconciliation. Each length has a clear point where the player can pause without losing the itinerary or replaying a prior service. The UI describes the stop as planned until a travel or site owner confirms arrival.

Every run sheet includes a start state, current constraints, expected confirmation source, unsupported-action fallback, and end-of-day summary. The day summary counts planned, reached, completed, declined, deferred, inaccessible, and unresolved stops separately. It must not present a single “success rate” that pressures the player to override individual choice.

### Field 02 expansion — visit state transition review

For each visit, authors answer:

- Who requested the stop, and is the request still current?
- Who is the intended recipient, and is the visit individual or group?
- What can be shown to other residents or team members?
- What owner verifies route availability?
- What owner verifies arrival?
- What command represents the service or conversation?
- Can the recipient stop or decline the interaction?
- What receipt proves the service or message happened?
- What follow-up is authorized?
- What state remains after the team leaves?
- If the team cannot reach the site, is there a supported way to notify the requester?
- How does a new request relate to the old one?

The answer may be “not currently supported.” That is useful evidence and should cause the stop to remain a content draft.

### Field 03 expansion — return and reschedule stop variants

| Stop variant | New evidence | Player action | Truthful result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Appointment moved | Resident proposes another time | Accept only through the current appointment owner | New time confirmed or proposal pending |
| Door unanswered | Team reaches the site, no contact occurs | Leave only an authorized notice or defer | Visit attempted; no service delivered |
| Group asks for private time | Group meeting reveals a private follow-up request | Offer available private slot | Request recorded, not completed |
| Route changes en route | Travel owner updates access before arrival | Continue, reroute, or return | Chosen travel result with no duplicate departure |
| Request withdrawn | Resident says the original request is no longer needed | Close through current request owner | Request withdrawn by its source |
| Team member unavailable | Duty owner changes the roster | Replan or defer | No silent substitution of staff |
| Supply not in stock | Canonical inventory quote returns none | Explain and ask whether a later check is wanted | No transfer and no invented substitute |
| Referral declined | Receiving service refuses the request | Share the result only with authorized audience | Referral not accepted |
| Message delayed | Current channel queues delivery | Wait or cancel if supported | Queued until delivered or cancelled |
| Recipient absent | Site reached but recipient is elsewhere | Request a new visit through existing route | Arrival recorded separately from contact |
| Second visit requested | Resident asks for later follow-up | Schedule or leave request pending | Follow-up state visible to its owner |
| No further contact | Recipient asks team not to return | Close repeat prompts where owner supports it | Preference retained, no penalty |

These variants add service realism without generating a second appointment or consent system.

### Field 04 expansion — three additional outreach arcs

**The public session and the private question.** A group asks the team to explain a service schedule. During the session, one participant asks about a personal concern in front of everyone. The player can offer a separate conversation, provide a general contact route, or decline to discuss private matters publicly. The group receives only the schedule information it requested. The participant later decides whether to continue. The ending measures clarity and respect, not the number of consultations.

**The unconfirmed destination.** A referral request names a receiving location that has changed operating hours. The team can check current site information, send a question through an available communication route, or explain that it cannot confirm the destination today. A resident may choose to wait, seek another known service, or withdraw the request. No path treats an unconfirmed referral as accepted. A callback shows whether new owner information arrived.

**The outreach ledger.** A new volunteer inherits a stack of notes with dates but no indication of whether residents agreed to follow-up. The player compares the notes, contacts only people with a current permission or request, and marks ambiguous entries for review. A resident appreciates the correction; another asks that the old note be removed from the active list while preserving the audit history if the current record owner supports it. The arc teaches that better records reduce unwanted visits.

### Field 05 expansion — encounter examples with source and result

1. A resident asks for a conversation; the team reaches the site; the resident declines after opening the door. Result: attempted visit, declined conversation, no follow-up unless requested.
2. A crew requests general information; the team arrives and delivers the session. Result: session completed; no individual health outcomes are inferred.
3. A household requests supplies; inventory shows no available stock. Result: request documented and unavailable; follow-up can be requested.
4. A visitor asks for a referral; the receiving owner is unknown. Result: referral draft remains unsubmitted; the player receives a clear explanation.
5. A message is accepted by the radio owner but not yet delivered. Result: queued message with a pending status.
6. A recipient agrees to one follow-up but not future recurring visits. Result: one authorized follow-up, no standing recurring permission.
7. A group meeting is moved to a reachable room. Result: updated meeting only after site/event owner confirmation.
8. A team arrives late after the recipient leaves. Result: arrival without contact, a new appointment only with consent.
9. A route is blocked before the team departs. Result: itinerary revised before travel; no false arrival entry.
10. A team member is removed from the roster. Result: replan or defer using duty owner, no fake replacement.
11. A resident asks to correct their name in a visit record. Result: correction follows the current identity/history authority.
12. A resident says the earlier concern has resolved. Result: source statement recorded; no automatic health-state mutation.
13. Two households ask for the same group session. Result: shared session offered only if both agree to group format.
14. A follow-up is no longer wanted. Result: current request closed and repeat prompt suppressed where supported.
15. The team returns unused supplies. Result: canonical inventory receives a transfer receipt.
16. A caregiver asks what may be shared with another group member. Result: audience preview before any share action.
17. A destination confirms a new visit window. Result: scheduled only through its owner.
18. No one answers the message. Result: status stays undelivered or unknown according to channel response.
19. A resident wants to report an access barrier rather than request care. Result: routed to current site/travel owner.
20. A player closes a request without service. Result: clear reason, preserved request history, no success reward.

### Field 06 expansion — evidence review by seam

| Seam | Evidence required before integration | Stop condition |
|---|---|---|
| Route | Current route query and refusal contract | No supported travel receipt |
| Roster | Current assignment and fitness gate | Panel invents a team role |
| Visit request | Current quest/request source | Prose-only request controls state |
| Health service | Named health owner and public command | New private health ledger required |
| Inventory | Quote, transfer, and rollback contract | UI reports stock not held by inventory |
| Consent | Current recipient or interaction contract | No way to honor refusal or audience |
| Message | Sent, queued, delivered, failed receipts | Toast implies delivery without owner result |
| History | Existing journal/save capture | New parallel visit history needed |

A seam can pass through an adapter but not through a generic UI callback that makes domain decisions. If a route needs a new persistent authorization record, the user or foreman must decide whether that belongs in the existing owner. The content plan cannot decide architecture by implication.

### Field 07 expansion — day overview and visit card microcopy

The overview header tells the player what the team is doing and when the next supported decision occurs. Each stop row has requester, location precision, status, and next action. The detailed card separates request text, permission, route, and service. The closeout panel asks only for the result the current owner can record.

Sample transitions:

- “Planned stop · route not checked”
- “Route checked · travel not started”
- “Team departed · arrival not confirmed”
- “Team arrived · contact not made”
- “Conversation declined · no follow-up requested”
- “Message queued · waiting for relay”
- “Referral offered · receiving service has not replied”
- “Visit complete · one follow-up requested”
- “Request withdrawn by resident”
- “No service recorded; the team could not reach the site”

The summary must not compress “declined,” “unavailable,” and “no answer” into “failed.” This distinction matters to both follow-up and player comprehension.

### Field 08 expansion — privacy and interruption review

A sensitive visit cannot appear in a public roster tooltip or group bulletin beyond the minimum needed for route planning. A public group session is described as general information. Individual response content remains private within whatever current authority permits. If no privacy boundary exists, the affected content is blocked until an owner defines one.

Urgent travel or service changes can use current notification policy, but routine appointment reminders should not interrupt play. A notification includes a source and an action. The player can defer noncritical reminders and find them later in the itinerary. Repeated declined visits never escalate urgency solely because no service was delivered. Screen-reader and controller behavior should preserve stop order, status, and focus without announcing private detail to an audience beyond the intended UI context.

### Field 09 expansion — daily routing and save/resume probes

For future verification, exercise: save before route validation; save after validation but before departure; save while traveling; save after arrival but before contact; save after a declined conversation; save after a message is queued; and save after a follow-up request. On resume, compare route identity, team identity, visit status, delivered message IDs, and active follow-up count. No completed stop can grant a second transfer or replay an encounter.

Measure only after the owning implementation exists: stop query count, route validation latency, panel refresh duration, long-history load, and save payload change. A reasonable architecture target is to avoid repeated global resident scans on every panel refresh, but concrete thresholds require a baseline. Any optimization must preserve the same command results and deterministic event order.

### Field 10 expansion — one complete day acceptance map

The implementation-ready example day contains three stops: a completed general session, a declined private visit, and a route-deferred request. It proves the panel can show distinct outcomes without a success score, that the third stop can be rescheduled only when the owner allows it, and that the first two do not repeat after reload. Optional content can include a queued message if the current radio route supplies a real receipt.

Handoff documentation records the requested package, current owner API and evidence, exact files claimed, existing save section, player flow, data validation, refusal copy, performance observation, and remaining unknowns. The integrator rejects the package if a panel invents a medical consequence, if a visit result is not durable where it needs to be, if declined contact resurfaces incorrectly, or if a message is shown as delivered without proof. A partial day may still be accepted as a bounded slice if each stop clearly reports what remains unimplemented.


## Pass 13 — Outreach cast, consent-aware dialogue, and follow-up quests

This pass adds character and story material for the outreach route. It does not encode diagnosis, treatment, or private health facts in narrative variables. Dialogue follows the visit and permission receipts accepted by current owners.

### Field 01 expansion — outreach characters with distinct boundaries

The mobile team should feel like a group with different skills and limitations, while any roster role remains the current duty owner’s authority. Candidate recurring voices include a route planner who trusts dated maps, a new volunteer who wants to visit every requester immediately, an experienced coordinator who pauses when consent is uncertain, a community host who prefers group information, and a resident liaison who knows that a private contact is safer for some topics. These traits inform dialogue but do not create hidden skill values.

Residents have their own schedules, preferences, and reasons for declining. The story does not reveal a private explanation just to justify a refusal. A person can say “not today” and remain sympathetic. Later participation depends on a new request, a supported appointment, or explicit consent, not on a player’s relationship score unless the current relationship owner supplies it.

### Field 02 expansion — dialogue states tied to real visit results

For every encounter, author variants for: request made; appointment proposed; appointment accepted; team departed; team arrived; contact not made; recipient declined; service or conversation completed; follow-up requested; follow-up declined; referral pending; referral rejected; and request withdrawn. These states are not permission to implement a new encounter state machine. Use the current owner’s vocabulary, and leave a variant unwired if that state is not representable.

Before a dialogue option is shown, verify its preconditions. “Share the summary” requires an authorized audience; “schedule a return” requires a supported scheduler; “send a message” requires a communication path. If the command is unavailable, explain the limitation in a neutral line and let the player choose another valid response. Dialogue never stores an action outcome before the owner returns.

### Field 03 expansion — optional outreach quest catalogue

| Quest | Situation | Player choice | Observable close |
|---|---|---|---|
| A Time That Works | A resident asks for another appointment hour | Offer supported windows or defer | Resident accepts, declines, or leaves proposal pending |
| The Quiet Table | A group session creates a private follow-up request | Offer a separate conversation | Individual request recorded without group disclosure |
| Notes Without Names | A volunteer has uncertain visit notes | Check source and audience before retaining | Current history owner confirms what is stored |
| Relay Window | A sender wants a message delivered outside the usual check-in | Use a supported queued message or explain delay | Queue or delivery receipt |
| No Second Knock | A resident asks not to be visited again | Record preference through current request/relationship owner | Repeat prompt is suppressed where supported |
| The Waiting Room | A meeting location becomes unavailable | Find an existing supported site | New location confirmed or meeting deferred |
| Stock Check | A household asks whether a supply is available | Query canonical inventory | Quote or refusal, no invented substitution |
| The Long Walk | A recipient cannot reach the proposed visit point | Check route and alternative site | Owner-confirmed alternative or clear barrier report |
| A New Question | A completed session leaves one unanswered question | Route it to a known current owner | Answer delivered or marked pending |
| Returned Kit | Supplies remain after an outing | Transfer through canonical inventory | Receipt confirms returned stock |
| The Unsent Note | A personal note has no approved delivery route | Ask sender what to do | Retained, discarded, or deferred per current record authority |
| Familiar Request | A resident repeats a request from a previous day | Link to earlier receipt before starting again | Existing request updated or new one accepted |

These quests focus on scheduling, privacy, access, and honest limitations. None awards a medical result for a conversation.

### Field 04 expansion — three multi-visit storylines

**The resident who sets the hour.** A worker has declined three daytime visits because their shifts change. The team can offer an evening slot only if roster and schedule owners permit it. The resident helps choose a public meeting point and asks that the time remain flexible. A later callback may show the meeting occurred, was rescheduled, or was declined; each outcome is presented without judgment. The story demonstrates that outreach adapts to people rather than measuring them against a fixed route.

**A question passed between crews.** A group asks about a service that the first team member cannot explain. The player can record the question, identify a current information owner, and choose whether to return personally or send a response through a supported channel. A second volunteer initially feels embarrassed at not knowing the answer, then helps prepare a clearer public handout. The task closes only when the current source answers or the question is explicitly left pending.

**The notebook with too many names.** A volunteer wrote names beside requests for follow-up but did not note who agreed to a return visit. The player should not schedule all of them. They review the source, seek permission only through valid contacts, and retain ambiguous notes according to current record policy. One resident confirms their request; another asks for the note to be removed from the active list; a third cannot be reached. The arc makes privacy a practical service skill.

### Field 05 expansion — short scene examples and follow-up branches

At a group session, a participant says, “Can I ask you something without the whole room hearing it?” The player can offer a private follow-up if a supported route exists, provide a general contact point, or explain that the team cannot discuss individual concerns in this setting. The next line should acknowledge the choice without exposing the topic to the group.

At a closed door, the volunteer asks, “Should we wait?” The coordinator can say, “We have arrived, but nobody has confirmed they want a visit today. Leave an authorized notice or return to the route.” This is an instructional line only if the team actually has that notice command. Otherwise the line names the supported deferment.

When a message is queued, the sender asks whether it arrived. The truthful response is: “It has been accepted for relay. We do not have delivery confirmation yet.” A later delivered receipt unlocks the callback. If the channel fails, the sender decides whether to retry, wait, or close the request.

### Field 06 expansion — content dependency handoff

Each quest packet identifies its current request source, route query, roster check, recipient-facing command, optional inventory or message action, history/save owner, and closeout screen. It lists unsupported states and which branch remains visible if an owner is missing. Health-related dialogue receives review from the project’s designated content owner and does not extend domain logic by itself. If a scene requires a new privacy or consent contract, stop and request an architecture decision before authoring it as playable.

### Field 07 expansion — route journal, individual history, and team debrief

The team debrief aggregates only visit outcomes allowed for that audience. The individual visit history remains distinct from the public route summary. A debrief should reveal operational lessons—route delays, unconfirmed delivery, schedule mismatch—without exposing private conversation content. The player can see which follow-ups remain open and why.

The route journal links to source notes. A text fragment opens from a visit card and returns to the same card on close. The final daily summary does not announce “everyone treated” or “community morale improved” unless an owner produces that fact. It reports service actions and unresolved requests in plain terms.

### Field 08 expansion — player-facing line review

Useful lines state a choice and its scope:

- “You can ask for one follow-up. It will not create a recurring visit.”
- “The group meeting shares general information; private requests stay separate.”
- “The channel has accepted the note. Delivery is still pending.”
- “The resident ended the conversation.”
- “The location is available according to the site owner, but the route is not confirmed.”
- “No supply transfer occurred.”
- “The resident asked the team not to return.”
- “The request remains open because its owner has not confirmed a next step.”

Review for stigma, coercion, false reassurance, assumptions about diagnosis, and pressure to complete every stop. Voice and text communicate the same essential information.

### Field 09 expansion — narrative callback lifecycle

A callback triggers from a specific receipt or a new request, not from a hidden quality score. Store only the owner identity or event reference required by the current quest/history authority. When a profile or line is retired, existing saves should retain a readable fallback through the current content migration path. Duplicate messages must not reopen a completed quest twice.

### Field 10 expansion — story packet acceptance

The content packet includes cast cards, relationship boundaries, scene states, optional quests, message samples, accessibility notes, event references, and one complete return-visit chain. Reviewers verify that a refusal branch is as complete as an accepted-visit branch, that no personal detail leaks into a public surface, that the service history reflects actual owner receipts, and that each ending can be resumed without replay. It remains a writing prototype until the appropriate current owners accept the interaction states.


## Pass 14 — Worked outreach day and route-to-follow-up evidence trace

This worked day makes the plan’s proposed route, visit, privacy, and rescheduling rules concrete. It is a design example only; every transition must still be mapped to existing owners.

### Field 01 expansion — morning briefing

The player opens the route board. Three requests are listed: a group asks for general information at Lantern School; one resident requested a private conversation at Glasshouse Row; and a worker asked for a return visit near the quarry. The route owner has not yet confirmed all three stops. The duty owner shows which team members are available. The player checks each request’s age and source.

The briefing explicitly says that group attendance is not individual consent, that the resident asked for privacy, and that the quarry route has an old access report. The player can plan the first two stops and defer the third pending route verification. No stock is consumed and no service is promised when the itinerary is drafted.

### Field 02 expansion — route validation and departure

Before departure, the route owner confirms the school and Glasshouse routes but cannot confirm the quarry approach. The board marks the first two as ready for travel and the third as deferred. The team roster owner accepts the itinerary. If either owner refuses, the player sees the reason and can revise the route.

The player starts travel. At this point, the system records only the owner-confirmed departure. The route board does not claim arrival. A save boundary before departure should resume with the itinerary selected but not in motion. A save boundary during travel must follow the existing travel owner’s behavior. The outreach panel must not write its own route progress.

### Field 03 expansion — first stop: group information

At Lantern School, the route owner reports arrival. The organizer confirms the room is available. The player begins the group session through the current interaction path. The session covers service hours and how to request a later visit. One participant asks a personal question. The player chooses to offer a private follow-up through the supported request route or provides a general contact point. The group record contains only the session and attendance result; the private request uses its proper owner.

The organizer asks whether the session is complete. The team records a completion only if the event owner accepts it. A later summary says “general information session completed; one private follow-up requested,” not “all concerns addressed.”

### Field 04 expansion — second stop: private visit declined

The team arrives at Glasshouse Row. The resident opens the door and says they do not want to talk today. The player chooses “Thank them and close the visit.” The system records arrival and decline separately if the current encounter contract supports both. No service is delivered. No follow-up is scheduled because the resident did not ask for one. The resident’s refusal does not lower a hidden team score or create a recurring reminder.

The volunteer asks whether to try again tomorrow. The coordinator replies that no repeat visit should be scheduled without a new request or supported permission. The player returns to the route screen; focus returns to the Glasshouse stop. The debrief lists “visit declined” as complete for the requested interaction boundary, not as a failed appointment.

### Field 05 expansion — third stop: route unavailable and rescheduling

The player reviews the quarry access note. The travel owner cannot confirm the route. The team does not depart for that stop. The player can send a message if a current channel exists, or leave the request pending and mark what evidence is needed. The requester receives no false “team en route” notice. Later, a new map report may enable a fresh decision, but the old itinerary is not silently revived.

The player chooses to queue an update to the worker. The channel owner returns “queued.” The stop detail says the message has not been delivered. A saved game at this point retains the queue status through the communication owner. Reload cannot send it twice.

### Field 06 expansion — follow-up and service boundaries

The participant from Lantern School confirms the private follow-up is still wanted. The player can schedule it only if the current appointment/quest owner exposes that action. The volunteer asks for permission before attaching any personal note to the group session. The player may leave the follow-up separate. The health owner, if called later, remains the only authority for health information. If no such access is exposed to the session, the scenario contains no health update.

At day end, unused items are returned through canonical inventory. The debrief reports confirmed transfers only. It also lists one queued message, one resident-declined visit, and one route-deferred request. Those are not merged into an aggregate success score.

### Field 07 expansion — expected screen sequence

1. Route overview with request age and owner-confirmed readiness.
2. Stop detail with request audience and permission.
3. Travel/departure status from the route owner.
4. Arrival result.
5. Interaction prompt with only supported actions.
6. Visit closeout with a clear outcome.
7. Optional follow-up authorization.
8. End-of-day reconciliation and debrief.
9. Service history links back to each receipt.

Back navigation does not undo departure or service. Closing a private detail returns focus to its stop row. The group debrief omits private follow-up content.

### Field 08 expansion — dialogue and notification sequence

The organizer says, “People asked for a time and a place to request a visit. Please keep the general schedule on the board.” The private participant asks to speak after the session. The player sees the audience of any note before saving. At the private residence, the resident says, “Not today.” The response is “Understood. We will close this stop.” The route notification says, “The quarry route is unconfirmed; no departure was made.” The sender of the queued message hears, “The channel accepted it for relay. Delivery is still pending.”

No line suggests that the resident’s refusal is a clinical risk or that the team has solved the group’s concerns. A muted-audio player can read each essential result in the interaction log.

### Field 09 expansion — save/load and long-history outcomes

Run the worked route with saves before briefing, after each route validation, after each arrival, after the declined visit, and after queuing the message. Compare itinerary, owner receipts, active follow-ups, inventory transfers, and message IDs. Confirm no repeated visit or transfer after reload. Open the route history after adding multiple prior outings and ensure the current day’s stops remain findable without loading every narrative note into the active screen.

### Field 10 expansion — review ruling for the sample day

The day is playable only if the route owner verifies departure and arrival, the interaction owner records group completion and decline without conflating them, message status is truthful, and follow-up permission has a current owner. If any of these fail, reduce the slice to the supported stops and mark the remainder blocked. The content can still be written, but the launch card must not imply full mobile service until the route and service receipts agree.


## Pass 15 — Outreach logistics, handoff quality, and repeat-route content

This pass adds non-clinical operational depth around packing, team handoffs, repeat visits, and route learning. It uses existing inventory, duty, travel, journal, and communication owners wherever the current contracts permit.

### Field 01 expansion — logistics should reduce uncertainty

Before departure, the player should be able to answer: who is assigned; which stops are accepted; what supplies are actually available; what access has been verified; what communications are pending; and what must return to the shelter. These are queries across existing owners, not a new mobile clinic inventory. A summary can be assembled for presentation, but it cannot become the authority for any item, assignment, or route.

Logistics are meaningful when they shape the itinerary. If a required supply is unavailable, the player can remove the stop, ask whether a non-supply conversation is still wanted, or defer the request. If a team member becomes unavailable, the duty owner controls reassignment. If a route changes, the travel owner controls the new path. The plan avoids a false “pack all” button that silently bypasses item ownership.

### Field 02 expansion — packing, checkout, and return record

A proposed outing checklist refers to canonical item IDs and transfer receipts. The player reviews a quote, commits a transfer through inventory, and sees which items were returned. A planned quantity is not a stock reservation. If the current inventory owner cannot reserve stock, the UI must call it an estimate. Partial checkout reports the items actually transferred, not the original requested list.

The return sheet distinguishes used, returned, damaged, missing, and never checked out only if the owner can represent those states. Otherwise, the plan reduces the sheet to current inventory transfers plus a narrative note. Team custody cannot become a second storage authority. Save/resume must not duplicate a checkout or return.

### Field 03 expansion — route preparation records

| Route case | Preparation action | Owner result | Outreach consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Known paved approach | Confirm current route and travel time band | Route accepted or unavailable | Stop may remain scheduled |
| Footpath with old note | Compare note age to map owner response | Current, outdated, or unknown | Mark access confidence clearly |
| Two linked stops | Ask travel owner for ordering | Route order returned or unsupported | Keep order as player preference if unsupported |
| Weather-affected leg | Query current travel/weather seam | Allowed, delayed, or refused | Reschedule only after owner result |
| Night return | Check duty and travel limits | Accepted or denied | Do not promise late visit |
| Group destination | Confirm room/site status | Site accepted or unavailable | Move only through event/site owner |
| Vehicle transfer | Check current vehicle capacity/status | Valid or invalid plan | No parallel vehicle counter |
| Remote contact | Use current radio route | Queued/delivered/failed | Avoid travel if message is sufficient |
| Second visit | Link to prior request | Still wanted or withdrawn | Do not duplicate open work |
| Supply pickup | Query inventory transfer | Items transferred or not | Explain any changed visit scope |
| Team substitution | Ask duty owner | Replacement accepted or refused | Update itinerary only on receipt |
| Closed destination | Query current site owner | Closed or unknown | Offer a supported alternate site |

The matrix names cases for integration review; actual route and weather rules remain with the existing owners.

### Field 04 expansion — logistics story arc

**The list that traveled too far.** A volunteer copied a supply checklist from another route and packed items no one requested. The player compares the checklist with current requests and canonical inventory. The team returns unused items and asks residents what they actually need. The volunteer later authors a better request-based list but cannot force it onto all routes.

**The driver’s margin note.** A driver wrote “take the upper track” beside a route, but the note is undated. The player compares the note with the map owner and decides whether to query the route, ask the driver, or delay the trip. A later return can validate the route only through a current travel result. The story shows that local knowledge is valuable while still requiring freshness.

**The crew handoff at dusk.** One team is late returning as another is preparing to leave. The player can wait for the current roster to accept the handoff, cancel the later outing, or send a message if supported. An optional conversation reveals that the outgoing crew needs rest, but no fatigue mechanics are added by the story. The closeout uses the duty owner’s actual assignment and the travel owner’s result.

### Field 05 expansion — logistics side quests

- Compare requested supplies with canonical stock.
- Return one unused item using the inventory owner.
- Verify the driver’s route note against current map evidence.
- Ask a resident whether a remote message would replace a visit.
- Identify which stops can share one route if travel owner supports it.
- Replan after a team member is unavailable.
- Tell a requester that a service cannot be delivered today.
- Ask the outgoing team to provide a dated handoff.
- Separate items planned from items transferred.
- Close a trip with a missing return receipt without inventing a loss.
- Revisit only requests still marked current by their source.
- Publish a route change through a supported communication channel.
- Confirm a group location before assembling participants.
- Review an itinerary after a site closure.
- Mark a route as unverified when its source is stale.
- Ask the next team to confirm delivery before repeating a message.

### Field 06 expansion — owner crossing and plan reuse

A route day can touch six existing authority families, but the mobile plan does not combine them. The handoff lists the current query and action for each: duty assignment; map/travel route; site availability; inventory transfer; encounter/request; message delivery. It identifies the host composition point that assembles read-only presentation where appropriate. Stateful changes route through their owning adapters and save sections.

Before promoting logistics stories, search current partial and integrated work for route optimization, expedition mode, vehicle capacity, roster safety, item return, and radio delivery. If an existing feature covers the same capability, use that feature and author a new branch only where it adds genuinely distinct player choices.

### Field 07 expansion — checklist panel and end-of-day summary

The checklist uses grouped statuses: planned, owner-confirmed, committed, completed, and needs review. A checkbox cannot move a gameplay state. It reflects an owner result. The player can collapse completed rows and keep unresolved returns visible. At day end, the panel provides a reconciliation: assigned crew; confirmed stops; unavailable stops; items checked out and returned; messages pending; and follow-ups accepted. Personal encounter details remain excluded from the operational summary unless the recipient permitted them.

### Field 08 expansion — non-shaming logistics language

- “The request is confirmed. The route is not.”
- “The item appears available; inventory has not transferred it.”
- “The team assignment changed. Review the route before departing.”
- “No return receipt exists for this item.”
- “The stop was removed from today’s route. The request remains open.”
- “The destination is closed according to its current owner.”
- “The message was queued; the requester has not received it yet.”
- “A visit is unnecessary if the resident prefers a message.”

UX review checks that the player can distinguish plans from commitments and that a missing supply does not appear as a player mistake.

### Field 09 expansion — route history and itinerary performance

As route histories grow, the current day’s list should remain fast and clear. Prior visits may be filtered by location, request source, and result. The active route should query only relevant owner states and avoid scanning all residents every frame. Return receipts should be joined by stable IDs, not fragile display names.

A performance profile includes many route records, several queued messages, multiple item transfers, and one unavailable owner. Measure panel opening, stop-detail refresh, end-of-day reconciliation, history search, and save size. Replay checks use stable stop ordering and ensure route retry does not duplicate departure or delivery.

### Field 10 expansion — complete route commissioning packet

The commissioning sample includes an accepted group session, a declined private visit, an inaccessible stop, one item checkout and return, and a queued message if existing owners support each action. It documents which rows are optional and what a reduced slice looks like when one owner is absent. Acceptance requires truthful separation of plans and results, durable state only through current save owners, and no duplicated inventory or medical history.


## Pass 16 — Outreach encounter acceptance examples

This closing tranche gives reviewers concise cases for verifying that visit language, logistics, and owner receipts stay aligned.

### Fields 01–03 — request and encounter cases

| Request | Valid distinction | Unsupported shortcut to avoid |
|---|---|---|
| “Please visit after my shift” | Request received versus appointment accepted | Treating a request as a scheduled visit |
| “Can you explain the service?” | Group information versus individual consultation | Treating attendance as personal consent |
| “Not today” | Arrival versus declined conversation | Calling the visit a health failure |
| “Can you bring supplies?” | Inventory quote versus committed transfer | Showing stock as delivered before transfer |
| “Please send this note” | Queued message versus delivered message | Showing a sent toast as recipient confirmation |
| “The path is difficult” | Access report versus route-owner result | Claiming a barrier has been repaired |
| “I no longer need the visit” | Request withdrawal versus missed appointment | Keeping a recurring reminder active |
| “Can someone return?” | Follow-up request versus accepted schedule | Inventing an appointment time |

Each case should be exercised through overview, detail, action preview, owner response, and end-of-day summary.

### Fields 04–07 — service-day results

A completed group session may still have unanswered questions. A declined individual visit is closed respectfully. An inaccessible stop remains pending only if the requester still wants it. A queued message remains in communication history until its owner reports delivery or failure. These results are shown independently; no daily score collapses them.

The player can re-open the source request from the summary. Focus returns to the stop row. Private follow-up text is absent from the group view. A missing owner produces an explanation and a draft state, not a fabricated action.

### Fields 08–10 — review cases

Reviewers test repeated refusal, message retry, stale route data, changed inventory between preview and commit, team reassignment, and save/reload after each durable result. They verify that the resident is not contacted again without a valid request, that transfer occurs at most once, and that a new itinerary is based on current owner results.

The handoff classifies each stop as content-only, owner-ready, integration-ready, or blocked. Only stops with an observable route and encounter receipt count as playable. A polished conversation with no supported action remains draft content, and the day summary must never imply service delivery merely to make the route feel complete.


## Pass 17 — One outreach stop record, fully annotated

A candidate visit called “Lantern School Information Session” demonstrates the separation between a route stop, a group activity, and individual follow-up. The working key is provisional. The request source is the organizer’s message. The intended audience is a group. The only promised service is general information through an already supported interaction. The stop does not promise a clinical assessment or treatment.

The opening card shows the request age, organizer, location, route confidence, expected audience, and what the session can cover. It clearly says attendance does not create individual consent. The route owner confirms travel and arrival. The event or encounter owner confirms the session. If no owner can record attendance or completion, the panel must use a narrative-only prototype and cannot claim the visit is operational.

During the session, a participant asks for a private conversation. The player can offer a supported follow-up, provide a general contact path, or explain that no private appointment can be scheduled through this route. The group record contains no private detail. The follow-up has a separate request ID and is visible only on a permitted individual surface. If an appointment owner is unavailable, the request remains pending and the group session may still close.

A delayed message from the organizer is queued through the current communication owner. The status reads “queued” until delivery is confirmed. The debrief lists the completed group session, the separate follow-up request, and the queued message. It never says “care complete” or “all attendees reached.” A declined later follow-up remains a valid closeout.

The route board, visit detail, interaction, closeout, and debrief must all agree on their status. Controller and keyboard review verifies that the private follow-up cannot be mistaken for a public group action. Text size, focus return, and notification behavior use current preference and UI contracts. The daily flow can be saved after arrival, after session completion, and after message queueing; reload must not duplicate the event or message.

The current owner trace identifies route/travel, group interaction, request handling, communication, history, and save paths. A missing owner disables only its dependent action when the primary session remains valid. If a missing consent or privacy contract makes a private interaction unsafe or unrepresentable, that branch and any promise to support it are blocked pending an owner decision.

The reviewer probes no arrival, organizer unavailable, group cancellation, one participant leaving, a private follow-up request, message delivery failure, and a save between queue and delivery. The final report counts only the session as playable if its owner receipts work. Follow-up scheduling and message delivery are reported separately. The record is rejected if the UI writes private facts into the public route log, repeats a declined request, or reports a service that did not occur.


The outreach day summary should also be useful to the team without turning into a private patient report. Show route readiness, available roster, accepted visits, pending messages, and canonical inventory transfers. Keep personal dialogue out of that operational summary unless the relevant owner and audience rules explicitly permit it. A coordinator can see that one visit was declined and that a follow-up request remains open without exposing why the resident declined. The player should be able to correct an itinerary before departure and understand whether the correction changes only the plan or commits a new owner action. This distinction is especially important when a route update arrives between selection and departure. The final receipt should identify the version of the itinerary that actually ran.

A route owner may update access after the team has already planned the day. The itinerary should identify whether the update arrived before departure, while traveling, or after the team reached a stop. Each case can produce a different truthful result, but the panel must not choose one by wall-clock comparison. Use the owner’s simulation event order and receipt. If travel was already underway, the current travel contract decides whether the team reroutes or returns. If the team had not departed, the itinerary can be revised before commitment.
